name: AGENTS.md Standard
description: Cross-tool, open Markdown convention for scoping project/agent context. A plain AGENTS.md file (a 'README for agents') gives AI coding agents build/test commands, code-style rules, and boundaries. Released by OpenAI in Aug 2025; adopted by 60,000+ repos and 28+ tools; contributed to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) in Dec 2025. Defines cascading/nested precedence (closest file wins) with a 32 KiB default concatenation cap. Directly informs how Labmate should scope instructions per workspace vs. globally.
user_identity_model: Not applicable. AGENTS.md is a file-based convention with no identity, authentication, or accounts. Authorship is whoever can commit the file to the repo (governed by the host VCS, e.g., Git/GitHub permissions). Global personal defaults live in a user-home file (e.g., ~/.codex/AGENTS.md) and are implicitly scoped to the local OS user; there is no auth model intrinsic to the standard. [uncertain]
multi_user_collaboration: Indirect / VCS-mediated. A repo-root AGENTS.md is shared with every contributor by being committed to version control, so team standards propagate automatically; subdirectory files let sub-teams (e.g., a payments package) ship stricter local rules. There are no built-in roles, permissions, or concurrency controls in the standard itself — collaboration and access control are inherited from the underlying repository/host. Personal global files (~/.codex/AGENTS.md) are per-developer and not shared.
workspace_definition: The 'workspace' is the directory tree of a project, anchored at the git root, with AGENTS.md files placed at any directory level. It is filesystem/repo-bound rather than an abstract cloud entity: the standard maps 1:1 onto a directory hierarchy. A workspace can contain many AGENTS.md files (OpenAI's own Codex repo uses 88), each scoping the subtree it lives in. This is explicitly the 'workspace = directory' model, contrasting with corpus-scoped products like NotebookLM.
workspace_session_binding: Not applicable in a session sense. AGENTS.md has no concept of sessions or conversations; it is resolved freshly per agent run based on the current working directory and the path from git root to cwd. The same files apply to any number of concurrent agent runs/sessions in that tree. Binding is path-based (cwd -> instruction chain), not session-based.
context_scoping: Three conceptual tiers of context: (1) global/personal defaults in ~/.codex/AGENTS.md (apply everywhere for that developer), (2) repo-root AGENTS.md (team-wide standards), and (3) nested per-directory AGENTS.md (subtree-specific overrides). At runtime the agent assembles the chain from global -> git root -> each intermediate dir -> cwd. Context is purely instruction text (build/test commands, style, boundaries); the standard does not scope tools, memories, or files beyond the textual guidance. Explicit user prompts override all file-provided context.
config_file_instruction_precedence: This is the core of the standard. Resolution walks the filesystem and concatenates every applicable AGENTS.md from global down to the current working directory: order = ~/.codex/AGENTS.md (global) -> <git-root>/AGENTS.md -> each <intermediate-dir>/AGENTS.md -> <cwd>/AGENTS.md. Files are joined with blank lines, empty files skipped, and the combined total capped at project_doc_max_bytes = 32 KiB by default (Codex). Because files closer to cwd are concatenated LATER, the closest file wins on conflict ('nearest-first'/'closest takes precedence'); a subdirectory file overrides the root rather than fully replacing the inherited chain. An AGENTS.override.md variant (Codex) takes precedence over the sibling AGENTS.md at the same level. Cross-tool: Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md and can pull AGENTS.md inline via '@AGENTS.md' import; Kilo Code orders it as agent-specific prompts > project custom instructions > AGENTS.md > global custom instructions > skills. The 32 KiB cap truncates SILENTLY (instructions near the end ignored, no TUI warning); it is raisable (e.g., project_doc_max_bytes = 65536 in ~/.codex/config.toml) at the cost of more token usage. Best practice: front-load critical instructions, keep the global file lean (<=5 KiB) so repo rules are not crowded out, keep each nested file scoped to its own directory, keep total under ~150 lines (beyond that yields diminishing returns and 20-23% higher inference cost), and write by hand (LLM-generated instruction files perform worse).
source_corpus_grounding_scope: Not applicable. AGENTS.md is an instruction/config convention, not a research-assistant corpus. It does not define a retrievable source set, does not perform RAG, and does not ground answers in documents. (Tangentially, the AGENTS.md file content is itself injected into the agent's context as instructions, but this is instruction-context, not source grounding.)
persistence_mechanism: Plain Markdown files persisted on the local filesystem and (typically) committed to the project's version control system (Git). Storage is mutable text edited in place; history/versioning is whatever the host VCS provides (commits = an append-only event log of edits). The personal global file lives in the user-home config dir (~/.codex/). There is no database, cache, or runtime store — the 'state' is just files on disk re-read on each agent run.
session_history: Not applicable. The standard stores no conversation/session history; it carries only standing instructions. Any history of how the instruction files themselves changed is provided externally by Git (diffable, browsable, exportable via the repo). Debugging which files are active for a given run is done at runtime, e.g., 'codex --ask-for-approval never "Summarize the current instructions."' or with --cd <subdir> to confirm nested overrides — but this inspects the active instruction chain, not stored history.
memory_layering: The closest analog the standard offers is a static, user-authored layering rather than auto-generated memory: personal global defaults (~/.codex/AGENTS.md) vs. shared durable repo rules (committed AGENTS.md) vs. localized subtree overrides (nested files). All layers are hand-authored, durable, and re-read each run; there is no ephemeral thread state and no auto-generated/learned memory. AGENTS.md is frequently paired with complementary specs (e.g., Anthropic's SKILL.md for packaged reusable skills) rather than providing memory itself.
search_retrieval_history: Not applicable. There is no history to search. 'Retrieval' is the deterministic filesystem walk that gathers the applicable AGENTS.md chain for the current directory; there is no full-text or semantic search and no cross-session reference mechanism beyond the files already on the path.
lifecycle_ttl_cleanup: Files are persistent until edited or deleted by a developer; there is no TTL, expiration, or automatic cleanup. The only runtime 'cleanup' behavior is the 32 KiB concatenation cap, which silently truncates the combined instruction text beyond the limit (and skips empty files) — a soft, per-run trimming rather than deletion of stored state. Lifecycle is otherwise entirely manual / VCS-driven.
sandbox_isolation_model: Not applicable to the standard itself; isolation is provided by whichever agent/tool consumes the file. Notably, AGENTS.md is a recognized security attack surface: NVIDIA research showed malicious AGENTS.md content shipped in dependencies can redirect agent behavior, exfiltrate data, or inject backdoors while hiding the change from human reviewers. This argues for treating AGENTS.md (especially from third-party/nested/vendored directories) as untrusted input and scoping/reviewing it carefully.
snapshot_state_restore: Not applicable. AGENTS.md captures no machine/environment state (no packages, env vars, or filesystem snapshot). Any 'restore' is just Git checkout of a previous version of the file. The standard concerns instruction text, not reproducible environment state.
parallelism_subagent_fanout: Not applicable to the standard; it is stateless config re-read per run, so any number of parallel agents/worktrees can resolve the same files independently and consistently. In monorepos, parallel agents working in different packages each pick up their nearest AGENTS.md, giving per-subtree behavior without coordination. The standard provides no coordinator or fanout mechanism of its own.
trigger_surface: Tool-agnostic: AGENTS.md is read on task start by 28+ agents/IDEs/CLIs regardless of how they are triggered — Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, VS Code, Gemini CLI, Jules, Devin, Factory, Amp, Aider, Windsurf, Zed, and others. The standard does not define trigger surfaces; each consuming tool brings its own (IDE, CLI, web, PR/issue automation).
implementation_stack: Deliberately minimal: a single Markdown file format with no schema, frontmatter, or required sections (free-form Markdown; common sections are setup/build, test, code style, and boundaries). Resolution logic lives in each consuming tool (e.g., Codex's filesystem walk + concatenation + 32 KiB cap configured via ~/.codex/config.toml project_doc_max_bytes; AGENTS.override.md handling). Governance/stack at the ecosystem level: contributed to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF, launched Dec 9 2025 by Anthropic, OpenAI, Block) alongside MCP and goose; 170+ member orgs by April 2026; platinum members include AWS, Anthropic, Block, Bloomberg, Cloudflare, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI. Spec/site at agents.md.
applicability_to_labmate: This is the canonical reference for how Labmate should scope instructions per workspace vs. globally. Directly transferable patterns: (1) Adopt a cascading precedence model: global (user/account-level) defaults < workspace-level instructions < more specific overrides, with the most specific scope winning on conflict and explicit runtime prompts overriding all — mirror this with a Labmate instruction document keyed by (scope, workspace_id) where workspace beats global. (2) Concatenate-and-cap: assemble the effective instruction set by merging applicable layers and enforce an explicit byte/token budget (AGENTS.md uses 32 KiB) — but AVOID NotebookLM/Codex's silent truncation: Labmate should warn/log when the budget is exceeded and front-load critical instructions. (3) Keep global lean: enforce a small global-defaults budget so workspace-specific rules are not crowded out. (4) Treat instruction content as an attack surface: since Labmate ingests instructions (potentially from shared Discord workspaces or external sources), validate/sanitize and bound the precedence of less-trusted scopes, per the NVIDIA AGENTS.md findings. (5) Persistence mapping: store the durable instruction layers in MongoDB (workspace doc + optional global/user doc), resolve and cache the merged effective-instruction blob in Redis keyed by workspace_id with a short TTL for fast per-message assembly, and stamp the resolved set into the LangGraph thread checkpoint so a session's effective instructions are reproducible. (6) Interoperability: because AGENTS.md is the de facto cross-tool standard, if Labmate ever reads repo context, honoring AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md precedence makes it compatible with the broader ecosystem.
